einzeiler: The remarkable life and legacy of Jackie Robinson breaking baseball's color barrier.
kurzfassung: Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's modern color barrier when he started for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947. Facing intense racial hostility and pressure, he relied on extraordinary restraint and athletic excellence to succeed. His pioneering career transformed baseball and left a lasting impact on the American civil rights movement.
stichpunkte: Began professional career in the black American leagues with the Kansas City Monarchs in 1945
Signed by Brooklyn Dodgers general manager Branch Rickey to break the modern color barrier
Endured severe racial abuse, hostile opponents, and threatened player strikes during his rookie season
Won the inaugural Rookie of the Year Award and the National League MVP in 1949
Pioneered a new style of play emphasizing speed and aggressive base running
Became a vital figure and symbol in the broader American civil rights movement
Achieved post-career success as a corporate vice president and bank co-founder
Honored posthumously with the Presidential Medal of Freedom and league-wide retirement of his number 42

kapitel.titel: Early Life and Entry into the Negro Leagues
Signing with the Brooklyn Dodgers and the Montreal Royals
Career Statistics, Playing Style, and Legacy

clips.text: The athlete felt dismayed by the chaotic organization and prevalence of gambling within his initial professional team environment.

clips.hook: A monthly salary of six hundred dollars
clips.text: The initial contract signed to enter the farm club system amounted to six hundred dollars per month, which equates to over eight thousand dollars today.

clips.hook: Four hits in five trips to the plate
clips.text: Despite an opposing catcher demanding that the pitcher throw at the newcomer, the batter delivered four successful hits during five plate appearances.
The harsh verbal attacks from an opposing manager accidentally served to solidify and bond the entire roster together.
Rather than seeking fame or celebrity status, the baseball legend simply demanded basic human respect.
